A comprehensive understanding of the intrinsic piezoelectric anisotropy stemming from diverse
chemical and physical factors is a key step for the rational design of highly anisotropic materials. We
performed high-throughput calculations on tetragonal ABO3 perovskites to investigate the overall
characteristics of their piezoelectricity and the interplay between lattice, displacement, polarization,
and elasticity. Among the screened 123 types of perovskites, the structural tetragonality is naturally
divided into two categories: normal tetragonal (c/a ratio < 1.1) and super-tetragonal (c/a ratio > 1.17),
exhibiting distinct chemical features, ferroelectric, elastic, and piezoelectric properties. Charge
analysis revealed the mechanisms underlying polarization saturation and piezoelectricity suppression
in the super-tetragonal region, which also produces an inherent contradiction between high
piezoelectric coefﬁcient d33 and large piezoelectric anisotropy ratio |d33/d31|. Both the polarization axis
and elastic softness direction are strongly correlated to piezoelectric anisotropy, which jointly
determines the direction of maximum longitudinal piezoelectric response d33. The validity and
deﬁciencies of the widely utilized |d33/d31| ratio for representing piezoelectric anisotropy were
reevaluated.
Over the past century, ABO3-type oxide perovskites encompassing a wide
range of compositions are among the most extensively studied functional
materials1, largely owing to their superior ferroelectric2,3 and piezoelectric4,5
properties arising from spontaneous polarization6. The switchable polar-
ization enables applications in ferroelectric information technologies7–9,
while the piezoelectric conversion of mechanical and electrical energy
underlies more broad technologies including ultrasonic transducers and
actuators10,11. The piezoelectricity, as a rank-3 tensor, involves complex
coupling between mechanical and electrical quantities described by
thermodynamics12.
The tetragonal phase of ABO3 perovskite is of particular importance
among the various structural phases. Most high piezoelectric response and
large ferroelectric polarization in experiments occurred in tetragonal phase
or mixed phases13. Here, we focus on the P4mm (space group) tetragonal
phase (other tetragonal perovskite phases are not ferroelectric or
piezoelectric) and a longstanding problem, piezoelectric anisotropy, which
is fundamentally important for modern engineering applications like
ultrasonic transducers14 and robotic metamaterials15. Highly anisotropic
materials can provide minimal noise from lateral vibrations, greatly redu-
cing manufacturing costs by skipping the precise control of the size of
pezoelectric vibrator, eg., the length/thickness ratio, to produce the clean
thickness resonance mode. Although its importance was acknowledged in
the 1990s16,17, the intrinsic factors governing anisotropy (e.g., composition
and geometry) remain unclear even for those well-studied P4mm ABO3.
Elucidating underlying mechanisms will facilitate high-anisotropy piezo-
electric material design and help the explanation of anomalous properties
near the morphotropic phase boundary (MPB)18 and along nonpolar
directions19,20.
Experimental piezoelectric data are largely lacking for most per-
ovskites. Moreover, reported values vary considerably due to different

motivated us to do a comprehensive study using high-throughput ﬁrst-
principle calculations24, which is a nascent ﬁeld endeavoring to speed up
time-consuminggrowthandcharacterizationexperiments25.Inthiscontext,
valuable insights into structural distortions, chemical characteristics,
polarization, and elastic properties, and the extent to which they relate to
piezoelectric anisotropy, can be gleaned to obtain an overall picture.
With this aim, we performed density functional perturbation theory
(DFPT) calculations on 123 tetragonal ABO3 compounds, including ﬁve
experimentally synthesized perovskites: BaTiO3 (BTO), KNbO3 (KNO),
PbTiO3 (PTO), BiCoO3 (BCO) and PbVO3 (PVO). Other perovskites
including KTaO3
26 and SnTiO3
27, which can potentially be synthesized as
strained thin ﬁlms or superlattices, were not considered as already synthe-
sized crystals in this work. Considering that the crystallographic phase of
ABO3 is intricately linked to lattice strain28 and the preparation process. For
instance, BiFeO3, a renowned multiferroic material, is rhombohedral but
can manifest as a tetragonal phase near the MPB29 and in its mixed
ceramics30. Thus, despite the experimental synthesis of only ﬁve single-
crystal P4mm ABO3 structures to date, many perovskites can in principle
exist in the tetragonal phase under speciﬁc conditions. Studies on lattice
deformation and interatomic displacement (Fig. 1a) show that the latter
dominates the structural tetragonality. The tetragonal phase stabilization
energy, displacement amplitude, polarization, elastic and piezoelectric
properties naturally cluster into normal tetragonal (lattice anisotropy c/a
ratio <1.1) and super-tetragonal (c/a ratio >1.17) groups with distinct che-
mical features. The polarization analysis reveals that its saturation in super-
tetragonal perovskites is related to the charge transfer limit between atomic
layers, which also results in the strong suppression of piezoelectric response
when c/a ratio >1.3.
The piezoelectric response depends on the selected crystallographic
coordinate system, while longitudinal surfaces provide a classical way to
visualize the piezoelectric anisotropy31. For tetragonal perovskites, two
classes of longitudinal piezoelectric response shapes were found, which are
closely related to polarization and elastic softness. Due to the constitutive
law, the elastic anisotropy signiﬁcantly impacts piezoelectric anisotropy.
The direction of maximum longitudinal response d33 is determined by the
softest elasticity direction and polarization axis in conjunction. Among the
studied perovskites, PTO exhibits the largest d33 from several favorable
conditions, including the moderate polarization switching energy, the
softest elastic properties among tetragonal perovskites, the coincidence of
polarization, softest elasticity, and maximum d33 directions. Our high-
throughput calculations reveal the challenge of obtaining both large d33 and
high |d33/d31| anisotropy concurrently. The dimensionless parameter
|d33/d31| ratio is widely used in the literature to characterize piezoelectric
anisotropy32–34, which, in fact, lacks rigor for most perovskites, as d31 is a
quantity that in principle depends both on the longitudinal polarization and
lateral stresses. |d33/d31| ratio is a constant that only works for 29 perovskites
along the particular polarization direction, whose polarization and max-
imum d33 directions are identical.
The following section ﬁrst provides an overview of the high-
throughput calculation framework and the quantities to be considered in
this work. The discussion begins with an analysis of lattice anisotropy and
spontaneous symmetry breaking to introduce two groups of P4mm per-
ovskites, namely tetragonal and super-tetragonal. Subsequently, we connect
polarization change to interatomic displacement and Born Effective Char-
ges (BECs) through detailed analysis. Then elastic anisotropy and visualize
the three-dimensional (3D) Young’s modulus were addressed to portray the
varying elastic softness. In the ﬁnal section, we introduce the conditions for
large piezoelectric coefﬁcient d33, analyze the reasons for suppressed
response in super-tetragonal perovskites, and revisit the physical meaning
and validity of piezoelectric anisotropy parameter |d33/d31| and its limita-
tions for tetragonal perovskites. The Methods section provides additional
computational details not covered in the preceding sections.

Both lattice deformation and interatomic displacement as lattice
instabilities can induce symmetry breaking due to the Jahn-Teller or
pseudo-Jahn-Teller effects37. However, whether these two major structural
instabilities in tetragonal perovskites are both spontaneous was usually
undistinguished. Analysis of the 127 ABO3 perovskites herein reveals lattice
deformation to be mostly nonspontaneous. Only four P4/mmm ACrO3
possess lower total energy than the cubic phase, while most P4/mmm ABO3
in our calculation revert to cubic after the lattice optimization. As shown in
Fig. 2a, when P4/mmm lattices were ﬁxed to the P4mm lattice constants, the
total energy increased signiﬁcantly, especially those with c/a ratio >1.17.
This further signiﬁes that lattice deformation is generally unfavorable for
structural tetragonality. In contrast, interatomic displacement is sponta-
neous for most tetragonal perovskites, except the four ACrO3. Figure 2b
shows the tetragonal stabilization energy (Et–Ec) to be proportional to
displacement amplitude, indicating that distortions in most tetragonal
ABO3 are indeed dominated by interatomic displacements (or optical
phonons), rather than the lattice deformation. The latter mostly occurs
passively due to the bond length changes caused by the former, as the
positive relationship shown in Fig. 2c.
The two structural instabilities also differ in their distributions, as
showninFig.2.Theinteratomicdisplacement,representedbyitsamplitude,
is continuously distributed over a range from 0.66 to 1.66 Å (Fig. 2c). In
contrast, the c/a ratio distribution and its impacts on total energy and
amplitude naturally divide into two categories (Fig. 2a, b). The normal
tetragonal perovskites like BTO, KNO, and PTO belong to the ﬁrst category
with c/a ratio <1.1, while PVO and BCO comprise the second super-
tetragonalcategorywithc/aratio>1.17.It’sworthmentioningthatBCOand
PVO were synthesized under high pressure38,39, indicating the more difﬁcult
preparation compared to conventional perovskites. From the perspective of
ferroelectricity, the latter may be known as hyperferroelectrics40 or pyro-
electricmaterials38aswellduetotheirpersistentpolarizationsandextremely
high ferroelectric switching energies. The discontinuity of c/a ratio dis-
tribution does not result solely from the ionic radius difference between
A-site and B-site ions (see the Goldschmidt tolerance factor distribution in
Fig. 2c). Although a smaller tolerance factor does promote greater lattice
tetragonality in the super-tetragonal region, it can’t fully account for the
observed discontinuity. Besides the ionic reason, the discontinuous tetra-
gonality more likely results from the chemical change, which involves a
combination of one B-O bond breaking and A-O bond strengthening, as
depicted in Fig. 2d, e.

orbitals. The macroscopic polarization value can be obtained by summing

As expected, Fig. 3a, b have illustrated that polarization generally
increases with larger displacement amplitude and c/a ratio. However, when
c/a ratio >1.3, the polarization increase tends to saturate, despite continued
growth in amplitude. This convergence cannot be attributed to cancelation
effects among the A-site, B-site, and O ions. As shown in Fig. 3c, all
polarization contributions from different ions increase overall with the c/a
ratio and begin to converge when the c/a ratio surpasses 1.3. The polar-
ization saturation stems from the BEC side. Indeed, as shown in Fig. S1, the
BECs trend toward convergence as the amplitude rises for c/a ratio >1.3.
When c/a ratio >1.3, volume is proportional to c/a ratio (Fig. S2). For a
converged Z*, since P is inversely related to Ω, the increase of P due to
interatomic displacement amplitude Δu is counteracted by the concomitant
increase in Ω. In otherwords, as the c/a ratio grows, charge transfer between
atomic layers becomes hindered(Z* converges), and the system approaches
a periodic parallel-plate capacitor with a ﬁxed charge amount on each plate.
When the planar charge is converged, the polarization of the capacitor no
longer climbs as the plate separation expands.

aligns with the polarization axis, it’s a constant. Moreover, the d31 is also a
constant (maximum and minimum d31 equal) when the applied lateral
stress is perpendicular to the polarization direction, independent of the
lateral orientation. Hence, |d33/d31| constitutes a suitable constant quanti-
fying the ratio between the overall maximum response from longitudinal
stress and the response along this longitudinal axis but from lateral stress.
This also appliestopolarizedtetragonalpolycrystallineand ceramic systems
with maximum d33aligningwith the overall polarization direction. They are
isotropic in the plane perpendicular to the polarization, so their d31 is
likewise constant along the polarization.
Onthecontrary,forBCO-likesingle-crystalperovskites,themaximum
d33 lies on a ring tilted from the polarization axis, as depicted in Fig. 5f.
Meanwhile, d31 is only constant whenthe longitudinal stress is polarization-
aligned. Although |d33/d31| along the polarization axis is still a constant, but
it doesn’t represent the direction of overall maximum d33. Moreover, for
other longitudinal orientations, |d33/d31| is a function that depends on the
lateral stress. Therefore, for BCO-like tetragonal single-crystal perovskites,
|d33/d31| is no longer an adequate parameter for characterizing piezoelectric
anisotropy. The same issue should also exist for polycrystalline and ceramic
systems lacking alignment between the overall polarization axis and
directions of maximum piezoelectric response.
In this work, high-throughput calculations were conducted for P4mm
ABO3 perovskites to comprehensively elucidate the mechanisms governing
intrinsic piezoelectric anisotropy spanning diverse chemical and physical
factors. Interatomic displacement drives the spontaneous structural

groups:tetragonal andsuper-tetragonal,exhibitingdistinctcharacteristicsin
ferroelectric switching barrier, polarization, elasticity, and piezoelectricity.
Polarization saturation and piezoelectric response suppression in the super-
tetragonal region result from the charge transfer limit, which also produces
an inherent contradiction between high d33 and large piezoelectric aniso-
tropy ratio |d33/d31|. The elastic softness direction and polarization axis
jointly control the 3D longitudinal piezoelectric response, with the former
playing a major role in determining the orientation of the maximum
longitudinal piezoelectric response. The piezoelectric coefﬁcient ratio
|d33/d31| cannot rigorously represent the anisotropy of most tetragonal
single-crystal perovskites. The condition for |d33/d31| utilization as a con-

longitudinal piezoelectric response. Overall, we hope this study serves as a
useful foundation for the rational design of intrinsically highly anisotropic
piezoelectric materials. These important intrinsic factors should also be
considered in multiscale modeling of all piezoelectric systems.
Methods
Density functional theory calculations
First-principles calculations were carried out using the Vienna ab initio
Simulation Package44,45 within the density functional theory framework.
The generalized gradient approximation exchange-correlation func-
tional in a version of the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof formulation opti-
mized for solids (PBEsol) was used46. An 8 × 8 × 6 Γ-centered k grid47, a
plane-wave energy cutoff of 550 eV, and the Gaussian smearing method
with a width of 0.05 eV were adopted. Spin-polarized calculations are
performed for magnetic systems (see Supplementary Material for
details). Hubbard-U parameters were kept the same with the Material
Project database35.
Density functional perturbation theory calculations
The elastic constants, piezoelectric constants, and Born effective charge that
determined via the DFPT routines48 were brieﬂy summarized as follows49.
When perturbations (displacements um, strains ηj or electric ﬁeld ε) are
appliedtoacrystal,theﬁrst-orderresponsestothetotalenergyEare(i)forces
Fm, (ii) stresses σj, and (iii) polarizations Pα. The pertinent second derivatives
of the total energy per unit volume can then be constructed: elastic stiffness
constants Cij = dσi/dηj, Born effective charges Zαm = dPα/dum, and piezo-
electric stiffness constants eαj = dPα/dηj. The eαj describes the change of
polarization Pα arising from a strain ηj, which equals the stress σj from a
changeofhomogeneouselectricﬁeldεα.Anotherequivalentdeﬁnition,more
commonly used in experimental literature, is the dαj = dηj/dεα that describes
thechangeofstrainηjfromaﬁeldεα,orpolarizationPαchangearisingfroma
stress σj. eαjand dαjdifferphysically, theycanbeeasilyconverted usingelastic
constants: eαj = Cijdαj vs. dαj = Sijeαj. Here, Sij = dηj/dσj are the elastic com-
plianceconstants,relatedbySij = Cij
−1.Computationally, Cijand eαjaremore
straightforward to obtain than the Sij and dαj. The visualizations of elasticity
and piezoelectricity were based on the framework of ELATE50.
DFPT is also extensively utilized for phonon calculations to assess the
dynamic stability of systems. In our case, of the 176 ABO3 structures under
consideration, only 51 manifest dynamic stability at the Gamma point. A
thorough phonon spectrum analysis across the entire Brillouin zone would
further reduce the number of dynamically stable systems. Speciﬁcally,
among the ﬁve experimentally synthesized systems, PTO, PVO, and BCO
demonstratedynamicstabilityattheGammapoint,whereasBTOandKNO
exhibit phonon imaginary frequencies reaching -3.6 THz. This discrepancy
arises because our DFPT-based phonon stability calculations reﬂect lattice
dynamics at zero Kelvin and do not account for stability at ﬁnite tem-
peratures, despite the fact that the phases of most perovskites differ between
room temperature and low temperatures. Consequently, we conﬁned our
evaluation to the mechanical stability, formation-energy stability, and
relative-energystabilityduringthescreeningprocess,whichisdeemedmore
rational than assessing phonon stability for ABO3 structures.
The reliability of the elastic and piezoelectric coefﬁcients
Given that the majority of P4mm ABO3 systems do not fulﬁll the criteria for
dynamic stability, the reliability of elastic coefﬁcients is somewhat con-
tentious. Although the computational methodology is straightforward,
potential energy surface instabilities result in some elastic coefﬁcients
deviating signiﬁcantly from those of real-world tetragonal ABO3 (such as at
room temperature). To mitigate this issue, we only selected mechanically
stable systems for high-throughput calculations to ensure that the majority
stiffnesstensorelementsarereasonable,especiallytheseprimarycoefﬁcients
c11, c33, c12, and c13, as evidenced by the comparison between calculated and
experimentalvaluesforBTO inTableSI.Thepiezoelectricstresscoefﬁcients
eαj, which are determined by the response of polarization Pα arising from a
strain ηj, are independent of dynamic instability. Conversely, piezoelectric
strain coefﬁcients dαj are not directly calculated but derived from calculated
piezoelectric stress coefﬁcients eαj and elastic coefﬁcients, thus inheriting a
similar issue to that of cij. Nonetheless, given the relative reasonableness of
the primary elastic coefﬁcients, the ﬁnal reliability of dαj, such as d33 and d31,
is deemed adequate for our discussions. Considering that we primarily aim
to provide a qualitative understanding of the piezoelectric anisotropy of
tetragonal ABO3, the presence of dynamic instability is not expected to alter
the overall conclusion.
